newsitem.title: FRANCE: Right leads, but slips a week from French poll.
newsitem.headline: Right leads, but slips a week from French poll.

text.p: The campaign for France's snap parliamentary election entered its last week on Saturday with the left gnawing at the ruling conservatives' lead and a third of voters still undecided.

The last four surveys released before a midnight (2200 GMT) ban on publishing opinion polls before the May 25-June 1 vote all saw the margin in favour of Prime Minister Alain Juppe's centre-right being slightly eroded.
A BVA survey said Juppe's coalition would win a 50-seat majority over the combined left, down from 52 a week earlier.
A CSA poll gave the conservatives a 39-seat majority in the National Assembly, down from 43 a day earlier and 80 a week ago.
Other polls by Ifop and Sofres, giving a range of seats, forecast a wider, but also slipping, majority for the right.
All the polls saw the left winning more votes than the conservatives in the first round, but ending up with fewer seats after the run-off because of the single constituency system.
Most agreed that the far-right National Front was poised to win a tiny foothold in parliament.
A 1993 landslide had given the ruling RPR-UDF coalition an unprecedented 385-seat majority in the 577-seat assembly.
The polls looked only at the 555 mainland constituencies and did not cover the remaining 22 overseas seats, most of which are held by the government.
The ban on publishing opinion polls in the last week before voting means no more election polls will be published until the election is over, as the run-off takes place a week after the first round.
As the polling machinery fell silent, Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin said voters "will thus have to make their decision in democratic meditation".

Surveys indicated that 23 to 38 percent of voters were still undecided, and unconfirmed reports said Gaullist President Jacques Chirac could intervene on behalf of the conservatives after returning from a state visit to China on Sunday.

Jospin said a second intervention in the campaign by Chirac, who earlier this month published a newspaper column to back the conservatives, would "distort democracy" and he would demand the right to respond.

Alarmed by reports that many conservative voters could stay away or cast blank ballots to mark their discontent with economic policies and political corruption, Juppe has warned that protest votes or abstention would favour the left and could return the Socialists after they were routed in 1993.
Foreign policy briefly burst into a campaign focusing on domestic issues on Saturday as Jospin branded the downfall of Mobutu Sese Seko a setback for the government.

"What is happening in Zaire certainly seals in a way the failure of France's African policy," he said. "The current government was wrong to put president Mobutu back in the saddle after we had tried to sideline him," he told reporters.
France clung to Mobutu long after other western powers had dropped him and was pushed to the diplomatic sidelines as Laurent Kabila's rebels advanced inexorably towards power.

There was no indication as to whether Mobutu would choose exile in France, where he owns a luxury Riviera mansion. Analysts said Paris was unlikely to offer him shelter until after the election for fear that his presence could become a campaign issue.
Former Socialist Party chief Henri Emmanuelli seized on the sale of 30 Airbus airliners to China during Chirac's state visit to snipe at the conservatives' privatisation policies.

He told a rally that bickering conservative leaders agreed on one thing: privatisation. "And what does Jacques (Chirac) sell in China? Private sector products? Not at all. Airbus planes, the jewel of Aerospatiale, a state company," he said.
